agastya.short: Canopus, the second-brightest star in the night sky, named after the sage Agastya.
full: Agastya lies far to the south, so from northern India it rises only a little above the horizon. The text gives it a place on the armillary sphere and a heliacal rising.

agni-star.short: A star in the constellation Taurus that the text names after the fire god Agni.
full: One of the text's fixed stars off the zodiac. Burgess identifies it with β Tauri, near Krittika (the Pleiades), whose ruling god is also Agni.

ahargana.short: The number of whole days that have passed since the epoch. Every planet's place is worked out from it.
full: Ahargana means “heap of days”. It is the count of civil days (sunrise to sunrise) from the epoch to the date you pick. The text builds it in steps: years gone by become months, extra leap months are added, the months become lunar days, and the dropped lunar days are taken away.
Once you have the ahargana, the mean place of any planet is a simple proportion: turns in a Great Age × ahargana ÷ days in a Great Age.

akshaya.short: Year 60 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “unfailing”.
full: Akshaya is year 60 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 34. Its name means “unfailing”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

amavasya.short: The 30th lunar day, which ends at the moment of new moon. The last day of the dark half.
full: Amavasya, the new-moon day, is tithi 30. It ends when the Moon catches up with the Sun. A solar eclipse can happen only at this moment.
Almanacs name the Pitris, the Fathers (ancestors), as its ruling gods.

anala.short: Year 50 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “fire”.
full: Anala is year 50 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 24. Its name means “fire”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

ananda.short: Year 48 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “bliss”.
full: Ananda is year 48 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 22. Its name means “bliss”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

angirasa.short: Year 6 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “of the sage Angiras”.
full: Angirasa is year 6 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 40. Its name means “of the sage Angiras”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

angular-diameter.short: How wide a body looks in the sky, as an angle. The Sun and Moon each look about half a degree wide.
full: The text gives the Sun's true diameter as 6,500 yojanas and the Moon's as 480, then turns them into minutes of arc. The faster a body moves that day, the nearer and bigger the text takes it to be.

antya.short: The day-measure: R plus the ascensional-difference sine (minus it in winter). The text uses it to turn the Sun's height into time.
full: Antya is the length on the day circle from the horizon to the meridian, in sine units. Chapter 3 uses it with the Sun's altitude to find the time since sunrise.

equations.caption: Plus when the Sun is north of the equator, minus when south.

anuradha.short: The 17th nakshatra, 213°20′ to 226°40′ of the zodiac. Its name means “success”.
full: Anuradha spans 213°20′ to 226°40′ of the sidereal zodiac, in Scorpio. Its name means “success”, and its ruling god is Mitra, god of friendship. Its junction star is usually identified with δ Scorpii.

apamvatsa.short: A faint star near Chitra (Spica) that the text lists among its fixed stars. Its name means “calf of the waters”.
full: Burgess identifies Apamvatsa with θ Virginis, close to Spica, and its neighbour Apas with a star six degrees north of it.

apas.short: A star near Chitra (Spica), listed with Apamvatsa among the text's fixed stars. The name means “waters”.
full: Burgess identifies Apas with δ Virginis, six degrees north of Apamvatsa.

apsis.short: The point of a planet's orbit where it moves slowest. The text calls it mandocca; the correction for it is manda.
full: The text pictures the apsis as an invisible being that pulls the planet toward itself, making it run ahead or fall behind its mean place. When the planet is at the apsis or opposite it, there is no pull and no correction.
The Sun's and planets' apsides crawl round the zodiac only a few hundred times in a whole kalpa. The Moon's turns much faster: 488,203 times in a Great Age.

arc.short: Half of the wheel: a semicircle used the same way to read the Sun's altitude.
full: The arc, dhanus, is a half-ring used like the wheel. It is lighter to handle and shows the same reading. The method comes from Burgess's notes.

arcminute.short: One sixtieth of a degree. The text measures most angles in minutes of arc.
full: The text splits a circle into 12 signs, each sign into 30 degrees, each degree into 60 minutes (kala), and each minute into 60 seconds (vikala). A full circle holds 21,600 minutes.

ardra.short: The 6th nakshatra, 66°40′ to 80° of the zodiac. Its name means “the moist one”.
full: Ardra spans 66°40′ to 80° of the sidereal zodiac, in Gemini. Its name means “the moist one”, and its ruling god is Rudra, the storm god. Its junction star is usually identified with Betelgeuse.

armillary-sphere.short: A teaching model of the sky: rings for the equator, ecliptic and horizon around a small Earth on an axle.
full: Chapter 13 tells how to build the sphere from wooden hoops, with the Meru staff as its axle and a small Earth globe in the middle. Hoops mark the Sun's daily paths, the ecliptic, the equator and the horizon. Turned by hand, or by water or mercury, it shows how the sky moves.
The Instruments page builds this sphere in 3D for any date, place and hour.

image.alt: A sphere made of rings: the horizon, the equator and the ecliptic, around a small Earth on a tilted axle.

ashadha.short: The 4th lunar month, about June–July. Named after the two Ashadhas, near which its full moon falls.
full: Ashadha is the 4th month of the lunar year, falling about June–July. Its name comes from the nakshatra the two Ashadhas: the full moon of this month falls near it.
When a leap month is added, it takes the name of the month that follows it.

ashlesha.short: The 9th nakshatra, 106°40′ to 120° of the zodiac. Its name means “the embrace”.
full: Ashlesha spans 106°40′ to 120° of the sidereal zodiac, in Cancer. Its name means “the embrace”, and its ruling god is the serpents (Sarpa). Its junction star is usually identified with ε Hydrae, in the head of Hydra.

ashtami.short: The 8th lunar day of each half-month: tithi 8 (bright half) and tithi 23 (dark half).
full: Ashtami means “eighth”. It is the 8th tithi of both halves of the lunar month: in the bright half the Moon is 84° to 96° ahead of the Sun, in the dark half 264° to 276°.
Almanacs name Shiva as its ruling god.

ashvina.short: The 7th lunar month, about September–October. Named after Ashvini, near which its full moon falls.
full: Ashvina is the 7th month of the lunar year, falling about September–October. Its name comes from the nakshatra Ashvini: the full moon of this month falls near it.
When a leap month is added, it takes the name of the month that follows it.

ashvini.short: The 1st nakshatra, 0° to 13°20′ of the zodiac. Its name means “horsewoman”.
full: Ashvini spans 0° to 13°20′ of the sidereal zodiac, in Aries. Its name means “horsewoman”, and its ruling god is the Ashvins, twin horsemen gods. Its junction star is usually identified with β and γ Arietis.

atiganda.short: The 6th of the 27 yogas: the Sun's and Moon's longitudes sum to 66°40′–80°. Means “great danger”.
full: Atiganda is the 6th yoga, in force while the Sun's and Moon's longitudes add up to between 66°40′ and 80°. Its name means “great danger”.

ayanamsha.short: The gap between the star-fixed zodiac used by the text and the season-fixed zodiac used in the West.
full: The Surya Siddhanta measures longitude from a fixed point among the stars. Western almanacs measure it from the spring equinox, the point where the Sun crosses the equator in March. Those two starting points are not the same, and the angle between them is the ayanamsha.

The text says the equinox does not drift forever. It swings back and forth like a pendulum, up to 27° either side of the fixed star point, over a cycle of 7,200 years. It was zero in 499 CE. Modern astronomy instead finds a steady drift of about 1° every 72 years that never reverses.
Add the ayanamsha to a sidereal longitude to get the tropical longitude shown in the Planet Positions table.

equations.caption: Take the cycle angle, fold it into a quarter circle (bhuja), then take three-tenths: at most 27°.
Turning a sidereal longitude into a tropical one.

image.alt: Two zodiac rings, one fixed to the stars and one to the seasons, offset by a small angle labelled ayanamsha.

ayushman.short: The 3rd of the 27 yogas: the Sun's and Moon's longitudes sum to 26°40′–40°. Means “long-lived”.
full: Ayushman is the 3rd yoga, in force while the Sun's and Moon's longitudes add up to between 26°40′ and 40°. Its name means “long-lived”.

bahu.short: In Chapter 10, the ‘base’ of the triangle used to draw the crescent. The app shows it as the crescent's width.
full: Bahu means “arm” or “base”. The text draws a right triangle between the Sun and Moon to find which way the lit part faces. Its base is the bahu.
The app reports the related width of the lit crescent, in minutes of arc: largest at the quarters and zero at new and full moon.

bahudhanya.short: Year 12 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “much grain”.
full: Bahudhanya is year 12 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 46. Its name means “much grain”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

balava.short: The 2nd of the seven movable karanas, which repeat eight times each lunar month.
full: Balava is one of the seven ‘movable’ karanas. After Kimstughna opens the month, the seven follow one another in a fixed order, Bava, Balava, Kaulava, Taitila, Garaja, Vanija, Vishti, eight times over. Each lasts half a tithi, the time the Moon takes to gain 6° on the Sun.

bava.short: The 1st of the seven movable karanas, which repeat eight times each lunar month.
full: Bava is one of the seven ‘movable’ karanas. After Kimstughna opens the month, the seven follow one another in a fixed order, Bava, Balava, Kaulava, Taitila, Garaja, Vanija, Vishti, eight times over. Each lasts half a tithi, the time the Moon takes to gain 6° on the Sun.

bhadrapada.short: The 6th lunar month, about August–September. Named after the two Bhadrapadas, near which its full moon falls.
full: Bhadrapada is the 6th month of the lunar year, falling about August–September. Its name comes from the nakshatra the two Bhadrapadas: the full moon of this month falls near it.
When a leap month is added, it takes the name of the month that follows it.

bhagana.short: One full turn of a planet around the zodiac. The text gives how many turns each planet makes in a Great Age.
full: Bhagana means one complete circuit of the stars, 360°. The text lists each planet's number of turns in a Great Age: 4,320,000 for the Sun, 57,753,336 for the Moon, 2,296,832 for Mars, 364,220 for Jupiter and 146,568 for Saturn. Mercury and Venus are given by the turns of their sighrocca.
These whole numbers are the heart of the text. With them, a planet's mean place on any day is a single proportion.

equations.latex: \text{daily motion} = \frac{\text{turns per Great Age} \times 360^\circ}{\text{civil days per Great Age}}

bharani.short: The 2nd nakshatra, 13°20′ to 26°40′ of the zodiac. Its name means “the bearer”.
full: Bharani spans 13°20′ to 26°40′ of the sidereal zodiac, in Aries. Its name means “the bearer”, and its ruling god is Yama, god of death. Its junction star is usually identified with 35 Arietis.

bhava.short: Year 8 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “being”.
full: Bhava is year 8 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 42. Its name means “being”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

brahma.short: The 25th of the 27 yogas: the Sun's and Moon's longitudes sum to 320°–333°20′. Means the creator god.
full: Brahma is the 25th yoga, in force while the Sun's and Moon's longitudes add up to between 320° and 333°20′. Its name means the creator god.
Brahma is also the creator god, whose day is a kalpa.

brahma-egg.short: The text's whole universe: a hollow sphere with the Earth at its centre and the planets' orbits inside it.
full: Chapter 12 describes creation from a golden egg. Its shell is the outer edge of everything. Inside, the orbit of the ether is the largest circle, then the stars, Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury and the Moon, with the Earth in the middle.

brahmahridaya.short: Capella, a bright yellow star in the constellation Auriga. The name means “heart of Brahma”.
full: One of the text's fixed stars away from the zodiac, given on the armillary sphere and among the stars with heliacal risings.

bright-limb.short: The lit edge of the Moon. It always faces the Sun; the horns point away from it.
full: The bright limb angle says which direction the lit edge faces, measured from north through east. The horns of the crescent lie at right angles to it.

budhavara.short: Wednesday: the day ruled by Mercury.
full: Budhavara is Wednesday. Its name comes from its ruling planet, Mercury. The ruler of the first hour after sunrise names the day, and the hours pass down the planets in order of distance, which gives the weekday order.
The app finds the weekday from the day count: the Kali epoch fell on a Friday.

carajya.short: The sine of the ascensional difference: how much longer or shorter than 12 hours the day is at your latitude.
full: At the equator, day and night are always equal. Elsewhere the Sun rises earlier and sets later in summer. The ascensional difference is that extra time on each side of 6 a.m. and 6 p.m. Its sine, the carajya, is the earth-sine divided by the day-radius, times R.

chaitra.short: The 1st lunar month, about March–April. Named after Chitra, near which its full moon falls.
full: Chaitra is the 1st month of the lunar year, falling about March–April. Its name comes from the nakshatra Chitra: the full moon of this month falls near it.
When a leap month is added, it takes the name of the month that follows it.

chaturdashi.short: The 14th lunar day of each half-month: tithi 14 (bright half) and tithi 29 (dark half).
full: Chaturdashi means “fourteenth”. It is the 14th tithi of both halves of the lunar month: in the bright half the Moon is 156° to 168° ahead of the Sun, in the dark half 336° to 348°.
Almanacs name Shiva as its ruling god.

chaturthi.short: The 4th lunar day of each half-month: tithi 4 (bright half) and tithi 19 (dark half).
full: Chaturthi means “fourth”. It is the 4th tithi of both halves of the lunar month: in the bright half the Moon is 36° to 48° ahead of the Sun, in the dark half 216° to 228°.
Almanacs name Ganesha as its ruling god.

chatushpada.short: One of the four fixed karanas, which fall once a month. It fills the first half of the new-moon tithi (Amavasya).
full: Chatushpada (“four-footed”) is one of the four ‘fixed’ karanas, which come once a month around new moon. It fills the first half of the new-moon tithi (Amavasya).

chitra.short: The 14th nakshatra, 173°20′ to 186°40′ of the zodiac. Its name means “the brilliant”.
full: Chitra spans 173°20′ to 186°40′ of the sidereal zodiac, in Virgo. Its name means “the brilliant”, and its ruling god is Tvashtar, the divine craftsman. Its junction star is usually identified with Spica.

chitrabhanu.short: Year 16 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “bright light”.
full: Chitrabhanu is year 16 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 50. Its name means “bright light”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

civil-day.short: A day counted from one sunrise to the next. The text's everyday day, and the unit of the day count.
full: The text knows several kinds of day. The civil day, called savana, runs from sunrise to sunrise. It is the day people live by, and the ahargana counts civil days.
A Great Age has 1,577,917,828 civil days. That is fewer than its sidereal days, because the Sun moves east among the stars through the year.

clepsydra.short: A water clock: a copper bowl with a small hole that sinks in a basin of water 60 times a day, once per ghati.
full: The text's water clock is a thin copper vessel with a hole in its base. Set floating in water, it fills slowly and sinks. Its size is chosen so that it sinks exactly 60 times in a day, once per ghati.
The Instruments page shows how much a clock that sinks a little too fast or slow would drift.

image.alt: A basin of water with a copper bowl floating on it. Water enters the bowl through a small hole in its base.

clime.short: One of the regions the text divides the Earth into around Meru, such as Bharata (India). Called varsha.
full: The text splits the Earth's northern half into regions, varshas, each with a name. India is Bharata; the four equator cities each lie in a different one. Burgess translates varsha as “clime”.

co-latitude.short: 90° minus your latitude: how far the pole is from the point overhead. Called lamba.
full: At the equator the co-latitude is 90°, at the pole 0°. The text uses its sine often, for example to find the corrected circumference and the length of the day.

conjunction.short: When two planets reach the same longitude and pass close together in the sky.
full: Chapter 7 finds when two of the star-planets have equal longitude, then how far apart they are north–south. The text calls a close meeting an encounter or ‘war’ (yuddha) and a wider one a meeting (samagama).
The app marks a separation under 1° as yuddha and under 5° as samagama.

corrected-circumference.short: The distance round the Earth along your own line of latitude. It shrinks toward the poles.
full: Circles of latitude get smaller away from the equator. The text finds yours by multiplying the Earth's circumference by the sine of your co-latitude and dividing by the radius. That is the same as multiplying by the cosine of your latitude.

equations.caption: φ = latitude of the place.

daily-motion.short: How far a planet moves along the zodiac in one day, in degrees and minutes of arc.
full: Each planet's mean daily motion comes from its turns in a Great Age divided by the days in a Great Age. The Moon moves about 13°10′ a day, the Sun about 59′, Saturn only about 2′.
The true daily motion changes from day to day, because the correction for the apsis (and, for the five star-planets, for the sighrocca) keeps changing.

dashami.short: The 10th lunar day of each half-month: tithi 10 (bright half) and tithi 25 (dark half).
full: Dashami means “tenth”. It is the 10th tithi of both halves of the lunar month: in the bright half the Moon is 108° to 120° ahead of the Sun, in the dark half 288° to 300°.
Almanacs name Yama as its ruling god.

day-length.short: How long the Sun stays above the horizon: 30 ghatis at the equinoxes, longer in summer, shorter in winter.
full: At the equinoxes day and night are both 30 ghatis (12 hours). Away from the equator, summer days are longer and winter days shorter. The text finds the difference from the Sun's declination and the place's latitude, as the ascensional difference (carajya).
Night length is simply 60 ghatis minus the day length.

equations.caption: The ascensional difference is added when the Sun is north of the equator, subtracted when south.

day-of-the-gods.short: Half a year. The gods at the North Pole see the Sun for six months, then lose it for six.
full: At Meru the Sun stays above the horizon while it is north of the equator, from the spring to the autumn equinox. That half year is a day of the gods, and the other half their night. For the demons at the South Pole it is the reverse. A year of the gods is one of our years.
The text also gives a day of the Fathers (a lunar month, on the Moon) and a day of Brahma (a kalpa).

declination.short: How far north or south of the celestial equator a body is. The Sun's goes from 24° north to 24° south in a year.
full: The celestial equator is the Earth's equator projected onto the sky. A body's declination, kranti, is its angle north or south of it. The text takes the Sun's greatest declination as 24°; the modern value is about 23.4°.
Declination decides how long the day is, how long the noon shadow is and, in Chapter 11, when the patas happen.

equations.caption: δ = declination, λ = tropical longitude.

image.alt: A circle with the equator across it and the pole at the top. A line to the Sun makes an angle δ, the declination, with the equator.

desantara.short: The correction for being east or west of the Ujjain meridian. It shifts each planet's mean place slightly.
full: The text's mean places hold at midnight on the Ujjain meridian. East of it, midnight comes earlier, so the planets have moved less; west of it, more. The text finds your distance from the meridian in yojanas, then scales each planet's daily motion by that distance over the corrected circumference.
The Correction to the Sun and Correction to the Moon on the Cosmography page are this correction.

equations.caption: Subtract east of Ujjain, add west.

dhanishtha.short: The 23rd nakshatra, 293°20′ to 306°40′ of the zodiac. Its name means “wealthiest”.
full: Dhanishtha spans 293°20′ to 306°40′ of the sidereal zodiac, in Capricorn. Its name means “wealthiest”, and its ruling god is the Vasus, gods of the elements. Its junction star is usually identified with β Delphini.

dhanu.short: The 9th sign, Sagittarius (the bow): 240° to 270° of the star-fixed zodiac.
full: Dhanu is the sign the West calls Sagittarius, the bow. In the text it covers 240° to 270° of the sidereal zodiac, which is offset from the Western sign of the same name by the ayanamsha. Its ruling planet is Jupiter.
It holds nakshatras 19 to 21, split into nine padas.

dhatri.short: Year 10 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “creator”.
full: Dhatri is year 10 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 44. Its name means “creator”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

dhriti.short: The 8th of the 27 yogas: the Sun's and Moon's longitudes sum to 93°20′–106°40′. Means “steadiness”.
full: Dhriti is the 8th yoga, in force while the Sun's and Moon's longitudes add up to between 93°20′ and 106°40′. Its name means “steadiness”.

dhruva.short: The 12th of the 27 yogas: the Sun's and Moon's longitudes sum to 146°40′–160°. Means “fixed, lasting”.
full: Dhruva is the 12th yoga, in force while the Sun's and Moon's longitudes add up to between 146°40′ and 160°. Its name means “fixed, lasting”.

dundubhi.short: Year 56 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “kettledrum”.
full: Dundubhi is year 56 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 30. Its name means “kettledrum”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

durmati.short: Year 55 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “ill-minded”.
full: Durmati is year 55 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 29. Its name means “ill-minded”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

durmukhi.short: Year 30 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “ill-faced”.
full: Durmukhi is year 30 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 4. Its name means “ill-faced”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

dvitiya.short: The 2nd lunar day of each half-month: tithi 2 (bright half) and tithi 17 (dark half).
full: Dvitiya means “second”. It is the 2nd tithi of both halves of the lunar month: in the bright half the Moon is 12° to 24° ahead of the Sun, in the dark half 192° to 204°.
Almanacs name Brahma as its ruling god.

dwadashi.short: The 12th lunar day of each half-month: tithi 12 (bright half) and tithi 27 (dark half).
full: Dwadashi means “twelfth”. It is the 12th tithi of both halves of the lunar month: in the bright half the Moon is 132° to 144° ahead of the Sun, in the dark half 312° to 324°.
Almanacs name Hari as its ruling god.

dyujya.short: The day-radius: the radius of the small circle the Sun traces in one day. It is R times the cosine of its declination.
full: When the Sun is on the equator it moves on the full circle of the sky, radius R. North or south of it, it moves on a smaller circle, the day-radius.

earth-circumference.short: The distance round the Earth at the equator: √10 × 1,600 yojanas, about 5,060 yojanas in the text.
full: The text takes the Earth's diameter as 1,600 yojanas and, instead of multiplying by π, multiplies by the square root of 10 (about 3.162). That gives about 5,059.6 yojanas.

earth-shadow.short: The cone of shadow the Earth casts away from the Sun. The Moon crossing it makes a lunar eclipse.
full: The text works out how wide the Earth's shadow is where the Moon crosses it. It starts from the sizes of the Earth (1,600 yojanas), Sun (6,500) and Moon (480), then scales by their speeds that day. The result is usually about 2½ times the Moon's width.

ecliptic.short: The Sun's yearly path across the sky. The zodiac is a band along it.
full: Over a year the Sun traces a great circle among the stars, the ecliptic. It is tipped 24° to the equator in the text. Planets stay close to it; their latitude is measured from it.
It is called the ecliptic because eclipses happen only when the Moon is on or near it.

ekadashi.short: The 11th lunar day of each half-month: tithi 11 (bright half) and tithi 26 (dark half).
full: Ekadashi means “eleventh”. It is the 11th tithi of both halves of the lunar month: in the bright half the Moon is 120° to 132° ahead of the Sun, in the dark half 300° to 312°.
Almanacs name Vishnu as its ruling god.

elongation.short: How far a body is from the Sun in the sky, as an angle. For the Moon it sets the phase and the tithi.
full: The Moon's elongation is its longitude minus the Sun's. It is 0° at new moon, 90° at the quarters and 180° at full moon. Each 12° of it is a tithi.
For the planets, elongation decides whether they can be seen at all. Too close to the Sun, they are lost in its glare.

equations.caption: Reduced to 0°–360°.

image.alt: From the Earth, one line points to the Sun and another to the Moon. The angle between them is the elongation.

epicycle.short: A small circle carried along a planet's main circle. The planet rides on it, which makes it speed up and slow down.
full: The text explains uneven motion with epicycles. The centre of the small circle moves steadily round the zodiac at the mean speed while the planet goes round the small circle, so seen from Earth it runs ahead or falls behind.
The text gives epicycle sizes in degrees. Unusually, they shrink a little between the ends of the odd and even quadrants.

image.alt: A large circle round the Earth carries a small circle, the epicycle. The planet on the small circle is seen away from its mean place.

epoch.short: A fixed starting moment from which time is counted, and at which the planets' places are known.
full: To find where a planet is, the text counts the days since a known moment and adds the motion made in those days. That known moment is the epoch.
The text itself counts from the creation or from the end of the Golden Age. The app uses the Kali epoch (3102 BCE), which the text allows: it says any convenient epoch may be used.

equator.short: The great circle halfway between the poles, on Earth or on the sky. At the equinoxes the Sun is on it.
full: The Earth's equator is 0° latitude. The celestial equator is the same circle projected onto the sky; declination is measured from it. The text calls it the equinoctial circle.
When the Sun stands on the celestial equator, day and night are equal everywhere.

equinox.short: One of the two moments a year when the Sun crosses the equator, and day and night are equal everywhere.
full: The spring (vernal) equinox comes around 20 March, the autumn equinox around 22 September. The text says the two equinoxes stand opposite each other on the zodiac.
The spring equinox is the zero point of tropical longitude. How far it lies from the text's star-fixed zero is the ayanamsha.

ganda.short: The 10th of the 27 yogas: the Sun's and Moon's longitudes sum to 120°–133°20′. Means “danger”.
full: Ganda is the 10th yoga, in force while the Sun's and Moon's longitudes add up to between 120° and 133°20′. Its name means “danger”.

garaja.short: The 5th of the seven movable karanas, which repeat eight times each lunar month.
full: Garaja is one of the seven ‘movable’ karanas. After Kimstughna opens the month, the seven follow one another in a fixed order, Bava, Balava, Kaulava, Taitila, Garaja, Vanija, Vishti, eight times over. Each lasts half a tithi, the time the Moon takes to gain 6° on the Sun.

ghati.short: A unit of time of 24 minutes. Sixty ghatis make one day.
full: The ghati, also called nadi or ghatika, is one sixtieth of a day, 24 minutes. Indian almanacs still give times as ghatis after sunrise. It splits into 60 palas (vinadis), and each pala into 6 pranas.
The text's clepsydra, a copper bowl that sinks in water, is made to sink once every ghati.

gnomon.short: An upright stick, 12 finger-widths tall, whose shadow tells direction, latitude and the time of day.
full: The gnomon, shanku, is set upright on level ground. Where its shadow tip touches a circle in the morning and afternoon gives an east–west line. Its shadow at noon on the equinox, the equinoctial shadow, gives the place's latitude.
The Gnomon shadow shown in the app is how long that shadow is, in the same 12-digit units.

image.alt: An upright stick on level ground. The Sun's ray passes its tip and casts a shadow along the ground.

grishma.short: Grishma, the hot season: the season while the Sun is in Taurus and Gemini, about mid-May to mid-July.
full: Grishma means the hot season. It lasts two solar months, while the Sun passes through Taurus and Gemini, roughly mid-May to mid-July. The text begins the round of six seasons when the Sun enters Capricorn.

guruvara.short: Thursday: the day ruled by Jupiter.
full: Guruvara is Thursday. Its name comes from its ruling planet, Jupiter. The ruler of the first hour after sunrise names the day, and the hours pass down the planets in order of distance, which gives the weekday order.
The app finds the weekday from the day count: the Kali epoch fell on a Friday.

half-duration.short: Half the time an eclipse lasts, from first contact to middle. Doubled, it gives the whole eclipse.
full: The text finds how long the eclipse lasts from the discs' sizes, the Moon's latitude and how fast the Moon gains on the Sun. It works in halves, from first contact to the middle and from the middle to the end, and refines each by repeating the step.

equations.caption: d₁, d₂ = diameters of the two discs, β = Moon's latitude, all in minutes.

harshana.short: The 14th of the 27 yogas: the Sun's and Moon's longitudes sum to 173°20′–186°40′. Means “delight”.
full: Harshana is the 14th yoga, in force while the Sun's and Moon's longitudes add up to between 173°20′ and 186°40′. Its name means “delight”.

hasta.short: The 13th nakshatra, 160° to 173°20′ of the zodiac. Its name means “hand”.
full: Hasta spans 160° to 173°20′ of the sidereal zodiac, in Virgo. Its name means “hand”, and its ruling god is Savitar, the Sun as giver of life. Its junction star is usually identified with δ Corvi.

heliacal-event.short: The first day a planet or star shows again at dawn or dusk after being hidden in the Sun's glare. Its last day is the setting.
full: A body too close to the Sun cannot be seen. As the gap grows it first shows low in the twilight, its heliacal rising. As the gap shrinks it vanishes, its heliacal setting.
The text gives each body a minimum distance from the Sun for this, from 8° for bright Venus to 17° for Mars.

image.alt: At dawn the Sun is still below the eastern horizon and a planet shows just above it, far enough from the Sun to be seen.

hemanta.short: Hemanta, early winter: the season while the Sun is in Scorpio and Sagittarius, about mid-November to mid-January.
full: Hemanta means early winter. It lasts two solar months, while the Sun passes through Scorpio and Sagittarius, roughly mid-November to mid-January. The text begins the round of six seasons when the Sun enters Capricorn.

hevilambi.short: Year 31 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “with golden ornaments”.
full: Hevilambi is year 31 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 5. Its name means “with golden ornaments”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

hoop.short: One of the rings of the armillary sphere. Each stands for a circle in the sky.
full: Some hoops are fixed (the horizon and the meridian). Others turn with the sky: the equator, the ecliptic, and small circles showing the daily paths of the Sun at each sign and of the stars.

hora.short: One hour (a 24th of the day), each ruled by a planet. The order of the rulers gives the order of the weekdays.
full: Take the planets in order of distance, from Saturn down to the Moon. The hours are ruled by each in turn. The ruler of the first hour after sunrise names the day, and every 24 hours the list moves on by three, which gives the weekday order Sun, Moon, Mars and so on.

horizon.short: The circle where the sky seems to meet the ground. Bodies rise and set as they cross it.
full: The horizon is the great circle 90° from the point straight overhead. The text's day length, rising times and heliacal risings all depend on when bodies cross it.

hour-angle.short: How far a body has turned past your meridian (the north–south line overhead), counted as time or angle.
full: When the Sun crosses your meridian it is noon and its hour angle is zero. As the sky turns, the hour angle grows by 15° per hour, or 6° per ghati. The text calls this the time from the meridian, nata.

illumination.short: The fraction of the Moon's face that is lit, from 0% at new moon to 100% at full moon.
full: The lit fraction is (1 − cos E) ÷ 2, where E is the elongation. The text instead gives the width of the lit part in digits, 12 digits being the whole disc.

equations.caption: E = elongation of the Moon from the Sun.

indra.short: The 26th of the 27 yogas: the Sun's and Moon's longitudes sum to 333°20′–346°40′. Means the king of the gods.
full: Indra is the 26th yoga, in force while the Sun's and Moon's longitudes add up to between 333°20′ and 346°40′. Its name means the king of the gods.
Indra is also the king of the gods, ruler of the nakshatra Jyeshtha.

intercalary-month.short: An extra lunar month added about every 2½–3 years so the lunar calendar keeps pace with the Sun.
full: Twelve lunar months fall about 11 days short of a year. When the gap grows to a whole month, a leap month, adhimasa, is added. It takes the name of the month that follows it.
The text gets the number of leap months in a Great Age by subtraction: lunar months minus solar months, which is 1,593,336.

ishvara.short: Year 11 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “lord”.
full: Ishvara is year 11 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 45. Its name means “lord”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

jaya.short: Year 28 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “triumph”.
full: Jaya is year 28 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 2. Its name means “triumph”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

julian-day.short: A plain count of days since 1 January 4713 BCE. The app uses it to turn any date, however old, into one number.
full: Calendars changed over the centuries, so comparing dates across them is awkward. Astronomers get around this by numbering every day in one unbroken count, the Julian Day. Day 0 began at noon on 1 January 4713 BCE.
The app turns every date into a Julian Day first. The Kali epoch, for instance, is Julian Day 588465.5. This is a modern tool, not part of the text.

junction-star.short: The one bright star the text picks in each nakshatra to mark its place. Called yogatara.
full: Each nakshatra is a small group of stars. The text names one star in each as the junction star, used to measure planets against. It gives each one's place as a polar longitude and a polar latitude.

jupiter.short: Jupiter, the star-planet whose 12-year circuit of the zodiac sets the samvatsara years.
full: It goes round the zodiac 364,220 times in a Great Age, about once every 11.9 years.
Its passage through the signs sets the 60-year samvatsara cycle.
It rules Thursday.

jyeshtha.short: The 18th nakshatra, 226°40′ to 240° of the zodiac, and also a lunar month. Its name means “the eldest”.
full: Jyeshtha spans 226°40′ to 240° of the sidereal zodiac, in Scorpio. Its name means “the eldest”, and its ruling god is Indra, king of the gods. Its junction star is usually identified with Antares.
It is also the 3rd month, about May–June, when the full moon falls near this nakshatra.

kalayukta.short: Year 52 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “joined with time”.
full: Kalayukta is year 52 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 26. Its name means “joined with time”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

kali-epoch.short: The moment the Kali Yuga began: midnight at Ujjain, 17–18 February 3102 BCE. The app counts days from here.
full: At the end of the Golden Age the text puts every planet together at the start of Aries (only their slow apsides and nodes are elsewhere). The Kali epoch is the matching moment at the start of the present Kali Yuga, fixed at midnight at Ujjain between 17 and 18 February 3102 BCE (Julian Day 588465.5).
Counting days from this moment rather than from the creation gives much smaller numbers while giving the same planet places.

kali-era-year.short: A year number counted from the start of the Kali Yuga in 3102 BCE. From late February, it is the year CE plus 3,102.
full: The Kali era counts years from the Kali epoch. The app's year turns on the epoch's anniversary, measured in the text's own years, which falls in late February. In mid-2025, 5,126 whole years have passed, so the current Kali year is 5127.
The text uses the count of years gone by to work out how many months and days have passed, and from those the day count (ahargana).

equations.caption: Its whole part plus one is the Kali era year.

kali-yuga.short: The fourth and shortest part of a Great Age, lasting 432,000 years. We are living in it now.
full: A Great Age is made of four ages: Krita (the Golden Age), Treta, Dvapara and Kali. Their lengths are 4, 3, 2 and 1 tenths of the whole, so the Kali Yuga is 432,000 years long.
The present Kali Yuga began in 3102 BCE. The start of it, the Kali epoch, is the fixed starting point for the day count used throughout this app.

kalpa.short: The longest cycle of time in the text: 1,000 Great Ages, or 4.32 billion years. Also called a day of Brahma.
full: A kalpa (Burgess translates it “Aeon”) is 1,000 mahayugas. That is 4,320,000,000 years. It is called a day of the creator Brahma, and his night is just as long.

The text counts the turns of every planet over a whole kalpa. Slow points, like the apsides and nodes of the planets, turn only a few hundred times in all that time, so they are given per kalpa rather than per Great Age.

kanya.short: The 6th sign, Virgo (the maiden): 150° to 180° of the star-fixed zodiac.
full: Kanya is the sign the West calls Virgo, the maiden. In the text it covers 150° to 180° of the sidereal zodiac, which is offset from the Western sign of the same name by the ayanamsha. Its ruling planet is Mercury.
It holds nakshatras 12 to 14, split into nine padas.

karana.short: Half a tithi: the time the Moon takes to gain 6° on the Sun. There are 11 karanas.
full: Each tithi has two karanas. Seven of them, Bava to Vishti, are ‘movable’ and repeat eight times in a month. Four are ‘fixed’ and appear once a month, around new moon: Shakuni, Chatushpada, Naga and Kimstughna.
Kimstughna holds the first half of the first tithi; the movable seven then cycle through the month; the other three fixed karanas fill the last three half-tithis before new moon.

equations.caption: 1 to 60 through the month, then mapped to the 11 names.

karka.short: The 4th sign, Cancer (the crab): 90° to 120° of the star-fixed zodiac.
full: Karka is the sign the West calls Cancer, the crab. In the text it covers 90° to 120° of the sidereal zodiac, which is offset from the Western sign of the same name by the ayanamsha. Its ruling planet is the Moon.
It holds nakshatras 7 to 9, split into nine padas.

kartika.short: The 8th lunar month, about October–November. Named after Krittika, near which its full moon falls.
full: Kartika is the 8th month of the lunar year, falling about October–November. Its name comes from the nakshatra Krittika: the full moon of this month falls near it.
When a leap month is added, it takes the name of the month that follows it.

kaulava.short: The 3rd of the seven movable karanas, which repeat eight times each lunar month.
full: Kaulava is one of the seven ‘movable’ karanas. After Kimstughna opens the month, the seven follow one another in a fixed order, Bava, Balava, Kaulava, Taitila, Garaja, Vanija, Vishti, eight times over. Each lasts half a tithi, the time the Moon takes to gain 6° on the Sun.

khara.short: Year 25 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “harsh”.
full: Khara is year 25 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 59. Its name means “harsh”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

kilaka.short: Year 42 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “wedge”.
full: Kilaka is year 42 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 16. Its name means “wedge”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

kimstughna.short: One of the four fixed karanas, which fall once a month. It fills the first half of the first tithi of the bright half.
full: Kimstughna (roughly “what a destroyer”) is one of the four ‘fixed’ karanas, which come once a month around new moon. It fills the first half of the first tithi of the bright half.

krantijya.short: The sine of declination, in the text's units (radius 3,438). It sets how far north or south the Sun is.
full: Krantijya comes from the Sun's longitude and the greatest declination of 24°. From it the text finds the day-radius, the earth-sine and the ascensional difference, and so the length of the day.

equations.caption: λ = tropical longitude, R = 3438.

krittika.short: The 3rd nakshatra, 26°40′ to 40° of the zodiac. Its name means “the cutters”.
full: Krittika spans 26°40′ to 40° of the sidereal zodiac, in Aries. Its name means “the cutters”, and its ruling god is Agni, god of fire. Its junction star is usually identified with the Pleiades.

krodhana.short: Year 59 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “wrathful”.
full: Krodhana is year 59 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 33. Its name means “wrathful”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

krodhi.short: Year 38 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “angry”.
full: Krodhi is year 38 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 12. Its name means “angry”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

kujya.short: The earth-sine: a length used on the way to the ascensional difference. It grows with both latitude and declination.
full: The earth-sine links the Sun's declination with your latitude. Multiply the sine of declination by the noon equinoctial shadow and divide by 12, the height of the gnomon.

kumbha.short: The 11th sign, Aquarius (the water-jar): 300° to 330° of the star-fixed zodiac.
full: Kumbha is the sign the West calls Aquarius, the water-jar. In the text it covers 300° to 330° of the sidereal zodiac, which is offset from the Western sign of the same name by the ayanamsha. Its ruling planet is Saturn.
It holds nakshatras 23 to 25, split into nine padas.

lagna.short: The point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at a given moment. Also called the ascendant.
full: As the Earth turns, the zodiac seems to rise in the east, one sign after another, in about two hours each. The lagna is the exact degree crossing the eastern horizon at the moment you choose.
The text finds it by adding up how long each sign takes to rise at your latitude (its rising time, in respirations).

image.alt: The sky dome over a horizon line. The zodiac arcs across the sky and meets the eastern horizon at a point marked as the lagna.

lambana.short: Parallax in longitude: how much earlier or later a solar eclipse's middle looks because of where you stand.
full: Lambana is the part of the Moon's parallax along the ecliptic. The text gives it as time, in ghatis. It is zero when the Sun is at the highest point of the ecliptic and grows toward the horizon.

lanka.short: An imagined city where the text's prime meridian meets the equator, south of Ujjain.
full: Lanka is the text's zero point on Earth: on the equator and on the meridian of Ujjain. The other three equator cities, Yamakoti, Romaka and Siddhapura, lie a quarter of the Earth apart from it. It is not modern Sri Lanka, which lies further east.
Many of the text's rules are first stated for Lanka, where the pole stars sit on the horizon, and then adjusted for latitude.

latitude.short: How far something lies north or south: of the Sun's path in the sky, or of the Equator on Earth.
full: In the sky, a planet's latitude, vikshepa, is how far north or south it is of the Sun's path (the ecliptic). The Moon's is never more than 4½° in the text; eclipses can only happen when it is small.
On Earth, a place's latitude, aksha, is how far north or south it is of the Equator. The text finds it from the noon shadow of a gnomon. Ujjain lies at about 23° north.

longitude.short: How far along a circle something lies. In the sky, a planet's place along the zodiac; on Earth, how far east or west.
full: Celestial longitude is measured along the zodiac (the Sun's yearly path) from its starting point, in signs, degrees and minutes. The text starts from the beginning of Aries, fixed among the stars.
Earthly longitude is how far a place lies east or west of a reference line. The text's reference line runs north–south through Ujjain; the correction for being off it is called desantara.

lunar-eclipse.short: When the full Moon passes through the Earth's shadow and darkens. It can only happen near the Moon's node.
full: At full moon the Sun, Earth and Moon line up. If the Moon is also close to a node, it enters the Earth's shadow and is eclipsed. Everyone who can see the Moon sees it at the same time.
The text finds the size of the shadow, how much of the Moon it covers (the magnitude) and how long the eclipse lasts (the half-duration).

image.alt: The Sun on the left, the Earth in the middle and its cone of shadow to the right, with the Moon inside the shadow.

lunar-month.short: The time from one new moon to the next, about 29.5 days. It holds 30 lunar days (tithis).
full: The Moon moves around the sky faster than the Sun. A lunar month is the time it takes to lap the Sun once, from new moon to new moon. It is always 30 tithis long.
Twelve lunar months are about 11 days shorter than a solar year. To keep the calendar in step with the seasons, an extra month is slipped in now and then.

magha.short: The 10th nakshatra, 120° to 133°20′ of the zodiac, and also a lunar month. Its name means “mighty”.
full: Magha spans 120° to 133°20′ of the sidereal zodiac, in Leo. Its name means “mighty”, and its ruling god is the Pitris, the Fathers (ancestors). Its junction star is usually identified with Regulus.
It is also the 11th month, about January–February, when the full moon falls near this nakshatra.

magnitude.short: How much of the eclipsed body is covered at the middle of an eclipse. Over the full width means total.
full: The text subtracts the Moon's latitude from half the sum of the two discs. The remainder is how deep the eclipse goes. When it is wider than the eclipsed body, the eclipse is total.
The app gives it as a fraction of the eclipsed body's diameter.

mahayuga.short: A Great Age of 4,320,000 years, made of four smaller ages. The text states most planet speeds per Great Age.
full: A mahayuga (Burgess calls it an “Age” or “Quadruple Age”) lasts 4,320,000 solar years. It is split into four ages in the ratio 4 : 3 : 2 : 1, the last and shortest being the Kali Yuga.
The text says every planet makes a whole number of turns (bhaganas) in one Great Age. That is what lets it find any planet's mean place by a simple proportion.

makara.short: The 10th sign, Capricorn (the sea-monster): 270° to 300° of the star-fixed zodiac.
full: Makara is the sign the West calls Capricorn, the sea-monster. In the text it covers 270° to 300° of the sidereal zodiac, which is offset from the Western sign of the same name by the ayanamsha. Its ruling planet is Saturn.
It holds nakshatras 21 to 23, split into nine padas.

manda-correction.short: The correction for a planet's slow apex (apsis). It turns the Sun's and Moon's mean places into true ones.
full: The text puts the planet on a small circle, an epicycle, whose centre moves at the mean speed. The planet's offset on that circle, worked out from its distance to the apsis, is the manda correction, called the equation of the centre in modern terms.
It is at most about 2°10′ for the Sun and 5° for the Moon.

equations.caption: Anomaly = apsis − mean place. The Sun's epicycle is about 14°, the Moon's about 32°.

mangalavara.short: Tuesday: the day ruled by Mars.
full: Mangalavara is Tuesday. Its name comes from its ruling planet, Mars. The ruler of the first hour after sunrise names the day, and the hours pass down the planets in order of distance, which gives the weekday order.
The app finds the weekday from the day count: the Kali epoch fell on a Friday.

manmatha.short: Year 29 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means the god of love.
full: Manmatha is year 29 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 3. Its name means the god of love.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

margashirsha.short: The 9th lunar month, about November–December. Named after Mrigashira, near which its full moon falls.
full: Margashirsha is the 9th month of the lunar year, falling about November–December. Its name comes from the nakshatra Mrigashira: the full moon of this month falls near it.
When a leap month is added, it takes the name of the month that follows it.

mars.short: Mars, one of the five star-planets. It circles the zodiac in about 687 days.
full: It goes round the zodiac 2,296,832 times in a Great Age, about once every 687 days.
The text lets it be seen only when it is at least 17° from the Sun.
It rules Tuesday.

masa.short: A month of the Indian calendar, named Chaitra, Vaishakha and so on. Each is a lunar month tied to a nakshatra.
full: The twelve months are lunar months. Their names come from nakshatras: a month is named after the nakshatra near which the full moon falls, so Karttika from Krittika, Chaitra from Chitra, and so on.
When a leap month is added, it takes the name of the month that follows.

mean-longitude.short: Where a planet would be if it moved at a steady speed. The first step before the corrections that give its true place.
full: The mean longitude pretends each planet moves at an even pace around the zodiac. It is found by a simple proportion from the day count: turns in a Great Age × days gone by ÷ days in a Great Age. The whole turns are thrown away and the fraction left over, times 360°, is the mean place.
Real planets speed up and slow down, and the five star-planets even seem to move backwards at times. The corrections of Chapter 2 turn the mean longitude into the true longitude.

equations.caption: R = turns in a Great Age, A = ahargana, C = civil days in a Great Age.

meena.short: The 12th sign, Pisces (the fishes): 330° to 360° of the star-fixed zodiac.
full: Meena is the sign the West calls Pisces, the fishes. In the text it covers 330° to 360° of the sidereal zodiac, which is offset from the Western sign of the same name by the ayanamsha. Its ruling planet is Jupiter.
It holds nakshatras 25 to 27, split into nine padas.

mercury.short: Mercury, the star-planet closest to the Sun. It is only seen low in the sky near dawn or dusk.
full: Its mean place is the mean Sun; its own quick circuit is given as its sighrocca's 17,937,060 turns in a Great Age.
It never strays more than about 28° from the Sun, so it is seen only near dawn or dusk.
It rules Wednesday.

meridian.short: The north–south line through the point overhead. A body crossing it is at its highest; the Sun crosses it at noon.
full: On the sky, your meridian runs from the north point of the horizon, through the point overhead, to the south point. On Earth, a meridian is a north–south line of equal longitude.
The text's prime meridian on Earth runs through Lanka and Ujjain.

meru.short: The golden mountain the text puts at the Earth's North Pole, home of the gods.
full: The text pictures Meru passing right through the Earth, with the gods at its northern end and the demons (asuras) at the southern end. Seen from Meru, the pole star is overhead and the Sun stays up for six months.
In the armillary sphere, the axle through the globe is called the Meru staff.

mesha.short: The 1st sign, Aries (the ram): 0° to 30° of the star-fixed zodiac.
full: Mesha is the sign the West calls Aries, the ram. In the text it covers 0° to 30° of the sidereal zodiac, which is offset from the Western sign of the same name by the ayanamsha. Its ruling planet is Mars.
It holds nakshatras 1 to 3, split into nine padas.

mithuna.short: The 3rd sign, Gemini (the pair): 60° to 90° of the star-fixed zodiac.
full: Mithuna is the sign the West calls Gemini, the pair. In the text it covers 60° to 90° of the sidereal zodiac, which is offset from the Western sign of the same name by the ayanamsha. Its ruling planet is Mercury.
It holds nakshatras 5 to 7, split into nine padas.

moon.short: The Moon, the fastest planet in the text. Its angle from the Sun gives the tithi and the phase.
full: It goes round the zodiac 57,753,336 times in a Great Age, about once every 27.3 days.
It is the nearest body and the fastest, about 13°10′ a day, so its place matters most for tithis, eclipses and parallax. The text gives it a diameter of 480 yojanas.
It rules Monday.

moon-phase.short: The Moon's changing shape through the month, from new to full and back, set by its angle from the Sun.
full: Half the Moon is always lit by the Sun. How much of that half faces us depends on the elongation. At 0° we see none (new moon), at 90° half (quarter), at 180° all of it (full moon).

moonrise.short: When the Moon crosses the eastern horizon. It comes about 50 minutes later each day.
full: The Moon moves east about 13° a day, so the turning sky takes longer each day to bring it up. At full moon it rises near sunset, at new moon near sunrise. Moonset is the same crossing in the west.

mrigashira.short: The 5th nakshatra, 53°20′ to 66°40′ of the zodiac. Its name means “deer's head”.
full: Mrigashira spans 53°20′ to 66°40′ of the sidereal zodiac, in Taurus. Its name means “deer's head”, and its ruling god is Soma, the Moon god. Its junction star is usually identified with λ Orionis, in Orion's head.

mrigavyadha.short: Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky. The name means “deer-hunter”.
full: In the story, the hunter chases the deer (Mrigashira, part of Orion). The text treats Sirius as one of its fixed stars off the zodiac.

mula.short: The 19th nakshatra, 240° to 253°20′ of the zodiac. Its name means “root”.
full: Mula spans 240° to 253°20′ of the sidereal zodiac, in Sagittarius. Its name means “root”, and its ruling god is Nirriti, goddess of misfortune. Its junction star is usually identified with λ Scorpii, in the Scorpion's tail.

naga.short: One of the four fixed karanas, which fall once a month. It fills the second half of the new-moon tithi (Amavasya).
full: Naga (“serpent”) is one of the four ‘fixed’ karanas, which come once a month around new moon. It fills the second half of the new-moon tithi (Amavasya).

nakshatra.short: One of 27 equal star divisions of the zodiac, each 13°20′ wide. The Moon passes through about one each day.
full: The text divides the zodiac into 27 nakshatras, or lunar mansions, named after star groups along the Moon's path. Each is 13°20′ (800′) wide and has four padas (quarters). Each also has a junction star, yogatara.
The Moon's nakshatra is one of the five parts of the panchanga.

equations.caption: λ = sidereal longitude.

nandana.short: Year 26 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “joyful”.
full: Nandana is year 26 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 60. Its name means “joyful”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

nara-yantra.short: A gnomon shaped like a man, used by day in clear sunshine to tell the time from the length of its shadow.
full: The text names this instrument, the nara-yantra, but the details come from the commentators. Like any gnomon, the shadow's length tells how high the Sun is, and from that the time since sunrise.

nati.short: Parallax in latitude: how far north or south the Moon seems shifted, which changes how much of the Sun it hides.
full: Nati is the part of the Moon's parallax across the ecliptic. It is added to or taken from the Moon's latitude before the text finds the solar eclipse's magnitude and duration.

navami.short: The 9th lunar day of each half-month: tithi 9 (bright half) and tithi 24 (dark half).
full: Navami means “ninth”. It is the 9th tithi of both halves of the lunar month: in the bright half the Moon is 96° to 108° ahead of the Sun, in the dark half 276° to 288°.
Almanacs name Durga as its ruling god.

node.short: One of the two points where a planet's path crosses the Sun's path. Eclipses happen only near the Moon's nodes.
full: A planet's path is tipped slightly against the Sun's path, so it crosses it at two points, the nodes. The text calls the node pata, and the Moon's rising node Rahu. The node draws the planet north or south, giving it its latitude.
The Moon's nodes slide backwards round the zodiac 232,238 times in a Great Age, about once every 18.6 years. A new or full moon close to a node brings an eclipse.

image.alt: The Moon's path, a wave, crosses the Sun's straight path at two points, the nodes. Its greatest distance from it is the latitude.

omitted-lunar-day.short: A lunar day (tithi) that starts and ends between two sunrises, so no civil day is named after it.
full: A tithi is a little shorter than a civil day. Now and then one begins after a sunrise and ends before the next, so it never holds a sunrise and is skipped in the calendar. That is an omitted lunar day, kshaya tithi.
In a Great Age there are 25,082,252 of them: the lunar days minus the civil days.

orbit.short: The circle a planet travels on. In the text, planets further out have bigger orbits and so move more slowly.
full: The text says every planet covers the same distance each day, about 11,858 yojanas. So a planet on a larger orbit takes longer to go round. From the Moon's orbit of 324,000 yojanas and each planet's turns, it works out all the orbits.
Their order, outward from the Earth, is Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, then the stars.

equations.latex: \text{orbit} = \frac{\text{orbit of the ether}}{\text{turns in a kalpa}}
equations.caption: Every planet travels the same number of yojanas a day.

orbit-of-ether.short: The largest circle in the text's universe: the distance every planet travels in a kalpa, about 18.7 quadrillion yojanas.
full: Multiply any planet's turns in a kalpa by its orbit and you get the same number. The text calls it the orbit of the ether, the edge the Sun's rays reach, and states it as 18,712,069,200,000,000 yojanas.
Working it out from the Moon, whose orbit is 324,000 yojanas, gives 18,712,080,864,000,000. The app uses this worked-out figure; the two differ by less than one part in a million.

equations.caption: The Moon's orbit times its turns in a kalpa.

pada.short: A quarter of a nakshatra: 3°20′ of the zodiac. The positions table shows it as p1 to p4.
full: Each nakshatra splits into four padas, so the zodiac holds 108. Nine padas make one sign exactly. The Nakshatra column shows which pada a planet is in, as p1, p2, p3 or p4.

paksha.short: Half of a lunar month: the bright half while the Moon grows, or the dark half while it shrinks. 15 tithis each.
full: The bright half, shukla paksha, runs from new moon to full moon. The dark half, krishna paksha, runs from full moon back to new moon. Tithis are named by their number within the half, so each name appears twice a month.

pala.short: A unit of time of 24 seconds: one sixtieth of a ghati. The text calls it a vinadi.
full: Sixty palas make a ghati, and each pala holds six pranas (respirations). The text's name is vinadi; later almanacs call it pala or vighati.

panchami.short: The 5th lunar day of each half-month: tithi 5 (bright half) and tithi 20 (dark half).
full: Panchami means “fifth”. It is the 5th tithi of both halves of the lunar month: in the bright half the Moon is 48° to 60° ahead of the Sun, in the dark half 228° to 240°.
Almanacs name the serpents as its ruling god.

panchanga.short: The Indian almanac. It gives five things for each day: tithi, vara, nakshatra, yoga and karana.
full: Panchanga means “five limbs”. For any day it lists the lunar day (tithi), the weekday (vara), the Moon's nakshatra, the yoga and the karana. Almanacs add the month (masa), the season (ritu) and the Jupiter year (samvatsara).
All five come from just two numbers, the true longitudes of the Sun and the Moon, and from the day count.

parabhava.short: Year 40 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “defeat”.
full: Parabhava is year 40 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 14. Its name means “defeat”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

parallax.short: The shift in the Moon's place caused by watching from the Earth's surface rather than its centre.
full: The text's planet places are as seen from the Earth's centre. The Moon is close enough that someone on the surface sees it shifted, most of all when it is low in the sky. For a solar eclipse the shift matters a great deal.
The text splits it into two parts: along the ecliptic (lambana, given as time) and across it (nati).

image.alt: Lines from the Earth's centre and from an observer on its surface to the Moon meet at a small angle, the parallax.

paridhavi.short: Year 46 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “running about”.
full: Paridhavi is year 46 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 20. Its name means “running about”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

parigha.short: The 19th of the 27 yogas: the Sun's and Moon's longitudes sum to 240°–253°20′. Means “iron bar”.
full: Parigha is the 19th yoga, in force while the Sun's and Moon's longitudes add up to between 240° and 253°20′. Its name means “iron bar”.

parthiva.short: Year 19 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “earthly”.
full: Parthiva is year 19 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 53. Its name means “earthly”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

pata.short: A moment when the Sun and Moon have equal declinations in a mirror-image position. Chapter 11 treats it as unlucky.
full: Chapter 11 describes two such moments, vyatipata and vaidhrita. At these times the text says the Sun's and Moon's rays mix and cause harm. They are avoided for ceremonies.
The same word pata also means a planet's node in other chapters. The Patas page shows when each begins, is at its middle and ends.

patala.short: One of the seven hollow worlds the text places inside the Earth, where serpents (nagas) and demons live.
full: Chapter 12 says the Earth globe holds seven cavities, the patalas. They are part of the text's picture of the universe and play no part in its calculations.

pausha.short: The 10th lunar month, about December–January. Named after Pushya, near which its full moon falls.
full: Pausha is the 10th month of the lunar year, falling about December–January. Its name comes from the nakshatra Pushya: the full moon of this month falls near it.
When a leap month is added, it takes the name of the month that follows it.

phalguna.short: The 12th lunar month, about February–March. Named after the two Phalgunis, near which its full moon falls.
full: Phalguna is the 12th month of the lunar year, falling about February–March. Its name comes from the nakshatra the two Phalgunis: the full moon of this month falls near it.
When a leap month is added, it takes the name of the month that follows it.

pingala.short: Year 51 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “tawny”.
full: Pingala is year 51 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 25. Its name means “tawny”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

planet.short: In the text, any of the seven moving bodies: Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus and Saturn.
full: The Sanskrit word graha means “seizer”. The text counts the Sun and Moon as planets. The other five are the star-planets, tara-graha, whose motion needs the extra sighra correction.
Uranus, Neptune and Pluto are too faint to see without a telescope, so they are not in the text.

plava.short: Year 35 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “boat”.
full: Plava is year 35 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 9. Its name means “boat”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

plavanga.short: Year 41 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “monkey”.
full: Plavanga is year 41 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 15. Its name means “monkey”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

polar-latitude.short: The star's distance from the ecliptic, measured along the circle from the celestial pole.
full: Paired with the polar longitude, it fixes the star's place. The text lists it in degrees north or south. For stars far from the ecliptic it differs noticeably from the modern ecliptic latitude.

polar-longitude.short: The text's way of giving a star's place: where the circle from the pole through the star meets the ecliptic.
full: Draw a line from the celestial pole through the star down to the ecliptic. The longitude of that point is the polar longitude, dhruvaka. It is not the same as the modern ecliptic longitude, which uses the ecliptic's own pole.

pole-elevation.short: How high the celestial pole stands above your horizon. It equals your latitude.
full: At the equator cities the two pole stars lie on the horizon; at Meru the north pole star is overhead. In between, the pole stands as many degrees up as your latitude.

prabhava.short: Year 1 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “origin”.
full: Prabhava is year 1 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 35. Its name means “origin”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

prajapati.short: Year 5 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “lord of creatures”.
full: Prajapati is year 5 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 39. Its name means “lord of creatures”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.
Prajapati, lord of creatures, is also the name the text gives one of its fixed stars.

prajapati-star.short: A star the text names after Prajapati, lord of creatures. Burgess identifies it with δ Aurigae.
full: One of the text's fixed stars off the zodiac, five degrees east of Brahmahridaya (Capella). Chapter 13 calls the same star Brahma.

pramadin.short: Year 47 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “careless”.
full: Pramadin is year 47 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 21. Its name means “careless”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

pramathi.short: Year 13 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “the tormentor”.
full: Pramathi is year 13 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 47. Its name means “the tormentor”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

pramoda.short: Year 4 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “delight”.
full: Pramoda is year 4 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 38. Its name means “delight”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

prana.short: A ‘respiration’: 4 seconds of star time. The text's smallest real unit of time.
full: The text calls time that can be felt “real” and says it begins with the respiration, prana or asu. Six pranas make a vinadi (pala). There are 21,600 in a sidereal day, the same as the minutes of arc in a circle, so one prana of time turns the sky by one minute of arc.

pratipada.short: The 1st lunar day of each half-month: tithi 1 (bright half) and tithi 16 (dark half).
full: Pratipada means “first step”. It is the 1st tithi of both halves of the lunar month: in the bright half the Moon is 0° to 12° ahead of the Sun, in the dark half 180° to 192°.
Almanacs name Agni as its ruling god.

priti.short: The 2nd of the 27 yogas: the Sun's and Moon's longitudes sum to 13°20′–26°40′. Means “fondness”.
full: Priti is the 2nd yoga, in force while the Sun's and Moon's longitudes add up to between 13°20′ and 26°40′. Its name means “fondness”.

punarvasu.short: The 7th nakshatra, 80° to 93°20′ of the zodiac. Its name means “good again”.
full: Punarvasu spans 80° to 93°20′ of the sidereal zodiac, in Gemini. Its name means “good again”, and its ruling god is Aditi, mother of the gods. Its junction star is usually identified with Pollux.

purnima.short: The 15th lunar day, which ends at the moment of full moon. The last day of the bright half.
full: Purnima, the full-moon day, is tithi 15. It ends when the Moon is exactly 180° from the Sun. A lunar eclipse can happen only at this moment.
Almanacs name Soma, the Moon god, as its ruling god.

purva-ashadha.short: The 20th nakshatra, 253°20′ to 266°40′ of the zodiac. Its name means “the former unconquered”.
full: Purva Ashadha spans 253°20′ to 266°40′ of the sidereal zodiac, in Sagittarius. Its name means “the former unconquered”, and its ruling god is the Waters (Apah). Its junction star is usually identified with δ Sagittarii.

purva-bhadrapada.short: The 25th nakshatra, 320° to 333°20′ of the zodiac. Its name means “the former lucky feet”.
full: Purva Bhadrapada spans 320° to 333°20′ of the sidereal zodiac, in Aquarius. Its name means “the former lucky feet”, and its ruling god is Aja Ekapada, the one-footed goat. Its junction star is usually identified with Markab (α Pegasi).

purva-phalguni.short: The 11th nakshatra, 133°20′ to 146°40′ of the zodiac. Its name means “the former reddish one”.
full: Purva Phalguni spans 133°20′ to 146°40′ of the sidereal zodiac, in Leo. Its name means “the former reddish one”, and its ruling god is Bhaga, god of fortune. Its junction star is usually identified with δ Leonis.

pushya.short: The 8th nakshatra, 93°20′ to 106°40′ of the zodiac. Its name means “nourishing”.
full: Pushya spans 93°20′ to 106°40′ of the sidereal zodiac, in Cancer. Its name means “nourishing”, and its ruling god is Brihaspati, teacher of the gods. Its junction star is usually identified with δ Cancri.

rakshasa.short: Year 49 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “demon”.
full: Rakshasa is year 49 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 23. Its name means “demon”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

raktakshi.short: Year 58 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “red-eyed”.
full: Raktakshi is year 58 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 32. Its name means “red-eyed”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

rashi.short: One of the 12 signs of the zodiac, each 30° wide, from Mesha (Aries) to Meena (Pisces).
full: The zodiac is split into 12 equal signs of 30°. In the text they start at a fixed point among the stars, so they do not line up with the Western tropical signs of the same names; they differ by the ayanamsha.
The Rashi column shows the sign a planet is in and how many degrees into it.

raudra.short: Year 54 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “fierce”.
full: Raudra is year 54 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 28. Its name means “fierce”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

ravivara.short: Sunday: the day ruled by the Sun.
full: Ravivara is Sunday. Its name comes from its ruling planet, the Sun. The ruler of the first hour after sunrise names the day, and the hours pass down the planets in order of distance, which gives the weekday order.
