The app finds the weekday from the day count: the Kali epoch fell on a Friday.

revati.short: The 27th nakshatra, 346°40′ to 360° of the zodiac. Its name means “wealthy”.
full: Revati spans 346°40′ to 360° of the sidereal zodiac, in Pisces. Its name means “wealthy”, and its ruling god is Pushan, guardian of travellers. Its junction star is usually identified with ζ Piscium.

ritu.short: One of the six Indian seasons, each two solar months long, starting from the Sun's entry into Capricorn.
full: The year has six seasons of about two months each: Shishira (cool), Vasanta (spring), Grishma (hot), Varsha (rains), Sharad (autumn) and Hemanta (early winter). The text begins them when the Sun enters Capricorn.

rohini.short: The 4th nakshatra, 40° to 53°20′ of the zodiac. Its name means “the red one”.
full: Rohini spans 40° to 53°20′ of the sidereal zodiac, in Taurus. Its name means “the red one”, and its ruling god is Brahma (Prajapati), the creator. Its junction star is usually identified with Aldebaran.

romaka.short: An imagined city on the equator, a quarter of the way round the Earth west of Lanka. Its name recalls Rome.
full: Romaka lies 90° west of Lanka. The name comes from the Romans; it echoes the text's claim, in Chapter 14, that astronomy was once taught in Romaka as well.

rudhirodgari.short: Year 57 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “spitting blood”.
full: Rudhirodgari is year 57 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 31. Its name means “spitting blood”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

sadharana.short: Year 44 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “ordinary”.
full: Sadharana is year 44 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 18. Its name means “ordinary”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

sadhya.short: The 22nd of the 27 yogas: the Sun's and Moon's longitudes sum to 280°–293°20′. Means “achievable”.
full: Sadhya is the 22nd yoga, in force while the Sun's and Moon's longitudes add up to between 280° and 293°20′. Its name means “achievable”.

samvatsara.short: A named year in a 60-year cycle set by the planet Jupiter. Each lasts about 361 days.
full: Jupiter takes about 12 years to go round the zodiac. A Jupiter year is the time it takes to move through one sign. Five of its circuits make a cycle of 60 years, each with its own name.
The text counts the names from Vijaya. Most almanacs, and this app's list, start the cycle at Prabhava, which makes Vijaya the 27th name.

equations.caption: Counted from Vijaya.

saptami.short: The 7th lunar day of each half-month: tithi 7 (bright half) and tithi 22 (dark half).
full: Saptami means “seventh”. It is the 7th tithi of both halves of the lunar month: in the bright half the Moon is 72° to 84° ahead of the Sun, in the dark half 252° to 264°.
Almanacs name Surya as its ruling god.

sarvadhari.short: Year 22 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “all-bearing”.
full: Sarvadhari is year 22 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 56. Its name means “all-bearing”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

sarvajit.short: Year 21 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “all-conquering”.
full: Sarvajit is year 21 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 55. Its name means “all-conquering”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

saturn.short: Saturn, the slowest and furthest star-planet in the text. It circles the zodiac in about 29½ years.
full: It goes round the zodiac 146,568 times in a Great Age, about once every 29.5 years.
It is the slowest and, in the text, the furthest of the planets, just inside the sphere of the stars.
It rules Saturday.

saubhagya.short: The 4th of the 27 yogas: the Sun's and Moon's longitudes sum to 40°–53°20′. Means “good fortune”.
full: Saubhagya is the 4th yoga, in force while the Sun's and Moon's longitudes add up to between 40° and 53°20′. Its name means “good fortune”.

saumya.short: Year 43 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “gentle”.
full: Saumya is year 43 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 17. Its name means “gentle”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

separation.short: The angle between two bodies in the sky at their closest, in degrees.
full: At a conjunction two planets share the same longitude but usually differ in latitude. The gap between them is the separation. The smaller it is, the closer the meeting looks.

seven-sages.short: The seven bright stars of the Big Dipper (Ursa Major), which the text places on the armillary sphere.
full: Indian tradition names the seven stars of the Plough after seven sages, the saptarshi: Marichi, Vasishtha, Angiras, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha and Kratu. The text asks for them to be fixed on the sphere.

shakuni.short: One of the four fixed karanas, which fall once a month. It fills the second half of the 14th tithi of the dark half.
full: Shakuni (“bird”) is one of the four ‘fixed’ karanas, which come once a month around new moon. It fills the second half of the 14th tithi of the dark half.

shanivara.short: Saturday: the day ruled by Saturn.
full: Shanivara is Saturday. Its name comes from its ruling planet, Saturn. The ruler of the first hour after sunrise names the day, and the hours pass down the planets in order of distance, which gives the weekday order.
The app finds the weekday from the day count: the Kali epoch fell on a Friday.

sharad.short: Sharad, autumn: the season while the Sun is in Virgo and Libra, about mid-September to mid-November.
full: Sharad means autumn. It lasts two solar months, while the Sun passes through Virgo and Libra, roughly mid-September to mid-November. The text begins the round of six seasons when the Sun enters Capricorn.

sharvari.short: Year 34 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “night”.
full: Sharvari is year 34 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 8. Its name means “night”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

shashthi.short: The 6th lunar day of each half-month: tithi 6 (bright half) and tithi 21 (dark half).
full: Shashthi means “sixth”. It is the 6th tithi of both halves of the lunar month: in the bright half the Moon is 60° to 72° ahead of the Sun, in the dark half 240° to 252°.
Almanacs name Kartikeya as its ruling god.

shatabhisha.short: The 24th nakshatra, 306°40′ to 320° of the zodiac. Its name means “a hundred healers”.
full: Shatabhisha spans 306°40′ to 320° of the sidereal zodiac, in Aquarius. Its name means “a hundred healers”, and its ruling god is Varuna, god of the waters. Its junction star is usually identified with λ Aquarii.

shishira.short: Shishira, the cool season: the season while the Sun is in Capricorn and Aquarius, about mid-January to mid-March.
full: Shishira means the cool season. It lasts two solar months, while the Sun passes through Capricorn and Aquarius, roughly mid-January to mid-March. The text begins the round of six seasons when the Sun enters Capricorn.

shiva.short: The 20th of the 27 yogas: the Sun's and Moon's longitudes sum to 253°20′–266°40′. Means “kind, auspicious”.
full: Shiva is the 20th yoga, in force while the Sun's and Moon's longitudes add up to between 253°20′ and 266°40′. Its name means “kind, auspicious”.
Shiva is also one of the chief Hindu gods.

shobhana.short: The 5th of the 27 yogas: the Sun's and Moon's longitudes sum to 53°20′–66°40′. Means “splendid”.
full: Shobhana is the 5th yoga, in force while the Sun's and Moon's longitudes add up to between 53°20′ and 66°40′. Its name means “splendid”.

shravana.short: The 22nd nakshatra, 280° to 293°20′ of the zodiac, and also a lunar month. Its name means “hearing”.
full: Shravana spans 280° to 293°20′ of the sidereal zodiac, in Capricorn. Its name means “hearing”, and its ruling god is Vishnu. Its junction star is usually identified with Altair.
It is also the 5th month, about July–August, when the full moon falls near this nakshatra.

shrimukha.short: Year 7 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “lucky face”.
full: Shrimukha is year 7 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 41. Its name means “lucky face”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

shubha.short: The 23rd of the 27 yogas: the Sun's and Moon's longitudes sum to 293°20′–306°40′. Means “auspicious”.
full: Shubha is the 23rd yoga, in force while the Sun's and Moon's longitudes add up to between 293°20′ and 306°40′. Its name means “auspicious”.

shubhakrut.short: Year 36 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “doer of good”.
full: Shubhakrut is year 36 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 10. Its name means “doer of good”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

shukla.short: “Bright”: the 24th yoga, the 3rd year of the 60-year cycle, and the name of the bright half of the month.
full: Shukla means “bright” or “white”. It names three different things. It is the 24th yoga, in force while the Sun's and Moon's longitudes add up to between 306°40′ and 320°. It is the 3rd year of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (samvatsara). And shukla paksha is the bright half of the lunar month, while the Moon grows.

shukravara.short: Friday: the day ruled by Venus.
full: Shukravara is Friday. Its name comes from its ruling planet, Venus. The ruler of the first hour after sunrise names the day, and the hours pass down the planets in order of distance, which gives the weekday order.
The app finds the weekday from the day count: the Kali epoch fell on a Friday.

shula.short: The 9th of the 27 yogas: the Sun's and Moon's longitudes sum to 106°40′–120°. Means “spear”.
full: Shula is the 9th yoga, in force while the Sun's and Moon's longitudes add up to between 106°40′ and 120°. Its name means “spear”.

siddha.short: The 21st of the 27 yogas: the Sun's and Moon's longitudes sum to 266°40′–280°. Means “accomplished”.
full: Siddha is the 21st yoga, in force while the Sun's and Moon's longitudes add up to between 266°40′ and 280°. Its name means “accomplished”.

siddhapura.short: An imagined city on the equator, on the far side of the Earth from Lanka. Its name means “city of the Perfected”.
full: Siddhapura lies 180° from Lanka. When it is noon at Lanka it is midnight at Siddhapura.

siddharthi.short: Year 53 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “one whose aims are met”.
full: Siddharthi is year 53 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 27. Its name means “one whose aims are met”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

siddhi.short: The 16th of the 27 yogas: the Sun's and Moon's longitudes sum to 200°–213°20′. Means “success”.
full: Siddhi is the 16th yoga, in force while the Sun's and Moon's longitudes add up to between 200° and 213°20′. Its name means “success”.

sidereal-day.short: The time the stars take to turn once around the sky: 60 ghatis, a little shorter than a sunrise-to-sunrise day.
full: A sidereal day is one full turn of the sky of stars. The text divides it into 60 nadis (ghatis), each nadi into 60 vinadis, and each vinadi into 6 respirations (pranas).
A Great Age has 1,582,237,828 sidereal days: exactly the civil days plus the 4,320,000 turns of the Sun.

sidereal-time.short: Time kept by the stars rather than the Sun. It tells which part of the sky is overhead.
full: A clock set to the stars gains about 4 minutes a day on a sun clock, because the Sun drifts east among the stars. Local sidereal time is the angle of the sky that has turned past your meridian.
The app uses it to place the rising sign (lagna) and to set the armillary sphere.

sidereal-year.short: The time the Sun takes to go once around the stars: 365.258756 days in the text.
full: The text's year is the time the Sun takes to return to the same place among the stars. Dividing the civil days in a Great Age by its 4,320,000 years gives 365.258756 days, only a few minutes longer than the modern sidereal year.
Because the text's year is tied to the stars rather than to the seasons, the seasons slowly drift against its months. The ayanamsha measures that drift.

sighra-correction.short: The large correction for the fast apex. It makes the star-planets seem to speed up, stop and go backwards.
full: This correction comes from a big epicycle driven by the sighrocca. For Venus the epicycle is over 260°. It can move a planet's place by tens of degrees.
Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus and Saturn need both the sighra and the manda corrections, applied in four steps.

sighrocca.short: The ‘fast apex’ that swings a planet back and forth as seen from Earth. It stands in for the Earth's own motion round the Sun.
full: For Mars, Jupiter and Saturn the sighrocca moves with the mean Sun. For Mercury and Venus the planet's own quick circuit is given as the motion of its sighrocca, and the planet's mean place is the mean Sun. Burgess translates the word as “conjunction”.
The pull of the sighrocca is what makes the star-planets seem to stop and move backwards (retrograde) at times.

simha.short: The 5th sign, Leo (the lion): 120° to 150° of the star-fixed zodiac.
full: Simha is the sign the West calls Leo, the lion. In the text it covers 120° to 150° of the sidereal zodiac, which is offset from the Western sign of the same name by the ayanamsha. Its ruling planet is the Sun.
It holds nakshatras 10 to 12, split into nine padas.

sine.short: In the text, half a chord of a circle of radius 3,438′. It is the modern sine times 3,438. Called jya.
full: Indian astronomers used the half-chord of a circle instead of the whole chord Greek astronomers used. That half-chord is our sine. Burgess writes “sine” for the Sanskrit jya, whose Arabic spelling was misread in Latin as sinus, the source of the word “sine”.
The text lists 24 sines at steps of 3°45′ (225′), in a circle whose radius is 3,438′. Values in between are found by straight-line interpolation.

equations.caption: 3,438 is the radius in minutes of arc: 21,600′ ÷ 2π.
The first entry of the table.

image.alt: A circle with an angle θ at its centre. The line from the arc straight down to the radius, half a chord, is the sine.

sobhakrut.short: Year 37 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “maker of beauty”.
full: Sobhakrut is year 37 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 11. Its name means “maker of beauty”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

solar-eclipse.short: When the new Moon passes in front of the Sun. What you see depends on where you are, so parallax must be found.
full: At new moon the Moon can pass between the Earth and the Sun. The text says the Moon covers the Sun like a cloud. Because the Moon is close to us, people in different places see it against the Sun in different spots. Chapter 5 corrects for this parallax.
The app computes the eclipse for the place you enter.

image.alt: The Sun on the left, the Moon in the middle casting a narrow shadow onto the Earth on the right.

solar-month.short: The time the Sun takes to pass through one sign of the zodiac, about 30.4 days. Twelve make a year.
full: A solar month begins when the Sun enters a new sign (a sankranti) and lasts until it enters the next. Because the Sun's speed changes through the year, solar months are not all the same length.
A Great Age has 51,840,000 solar months, twelve for each of its 4,320,000 years.

solstice.short: One of the two moments a year when the Sun is furthest north or south, giving the longest and shortest days.
full: At the June solstice the Sun is 24° north of the equator (in the text) and the day is longest north of it; at the December solstice it is 24° south. From the entry into Capricorn the Sun moves north for six months (uttarayana), then south (dakshinayana).

somavara.short: Monday: the day ruled by the Moon.
full: Somavara is Monday. Its name comes from its ruling planet, the Moon. The ruler of the first hour after sunrise names the day, and the hours pass down the planets in order of distance, which gives the weekday order.
The app finds the weekday from the day count: the Kali epoch fell on a Friday.

staff.short: A straight rod held toward the Sun. The length of the chord from its tip to the horizon gives the time of day.
full: The staff, yashti, is one of the text's simple time-keepers. Burgess's notes explain how the length from its tip to the horizon point below the Sun is turned into ghatis since sunrise. The method comes from the commentary, not the verses.

sukarma.short: The 7th of the 27 yogas: the Sun's and Moon's longitudes sum to 80°–93°20′. Means “good deeds”.
full: Sukarma is the 7th yoga, in force while the Sun's and Moon's longitudes add up to between 80° and 93°20′. Its name means “good deeds”.

sun.short: The Sun, which the text counts as a planet. Its yearly circuit of the zodiac sets the solar months and year.
full: It goes round the zodiac 4,320,000 times in a Great Age, once a year.
Its true place needs only the correction for its apsis, at most about 2°10′. The text gives it a diameter of 6,500 yojanas.
It rules Sunday.

surya-siddhanta.short: An old Indian astronomy text that gives rules for finding where the Sun, Moon and planets are on any day.
full: The Surya Siddhanta is a Sanskrit astronomy text in verse, in fourteen chapters. Its present form is usually dated to around 400–500 CE. It explains time, the motions of the planets, eclipses, the stars and the instruments used to observe them.

This app follows Ebenezer Burgess's 1860 English translation. Every number is worked out from the text's own rules, not from a modern star table, so results can differ a little from modern values. The text is doing exactly what it says; it is not a bug.

svabhanu.short: Year 17 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “self-shining”.
full: Svabhanu is year 17 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 51. Its name means “self-shining”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

svati.short: The 15th nakshatra, 186°40′ to 200° of the zodiac. Its name means said to mean “sword”.
full: Svati spans 186°40′ to 200° of the sidereal zodiac, in Libra. Its name means said to mean “sword”, and its ruling god is Vayu, the wind god. Its junction star is usually identified with Arcturus.

taitila.short: The 4th of the seven movable karanas, which repeat eight times each lunar month.
full: Taitila is one of the seven ‘movable’ karanas. After Kimstughna opens the month, the seven follow one another in a fixed order, Bava, Balava, Kaulava, Taitila, Garaja, Vanija, Vishti, eight times over. Each lasts half a tithi, the time the Moon takes to gain 6° on the Sun.

tarana.short: Year 18 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “rescuing”.
full: Tarana is year 18 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 52. Its name means “rescuing”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

tithi.short: A lunar day: the time the Moon takes to gain 12° on the Sun. A lunar month has 30 of them.
full: Each day the Moon pulls about 12° further ahead of the Sun. A tithi ends each time that gap grows by another 12°. Because the Moon's speed changes, a tithi lasts anywhere from about 20 to 27 hours, so it does not match the civil day.

Tithis 1–15 make the bright half of the month (waxing), ending at full moon (Purnima). Tithis 16–30 make the dark half (waning), ending at new moon (Amavasya). The tithi in force at sunrise names the day.

totality.short: The part of an eclipse when the body is fully covered. Its half-length is the text's vimarda.
full: A total eclipse has an extra stage in the middle when the whole body is hidden. The text finds half its length just as for the whole eclipse, using the difference of the discs instead of their sum.

trayodashi.short: The 13th lunar day of each half-month: tithi 13 (bright half) and tithi 28 (dark half).
full: Trayodashi means “thirteenth”. It is the 13th tithi of both halves of the lunar month: in the bright half the Moon is 144° to 156° ahead of the Sun, in the dark half 324° to 336°.
Almanacs name Kama as its ruling god.

trepidation.short: The text's idea that the equinox swings back and forth by up to 27° over 7,200 years, instead of drifting steadily.
full: The text holds that the equinox moves like a pendulum. It swings 27° one way and then back over a cycle of 7,200 years, with 600 swings in a Great Age. Burgess calls this a libration.

Modern astronomy instead finds a steady westward drift, the precession of the equinoxes, of about 1° every 72 years. The app follows the text, so its ayanamsha grows at about the right rate today but would turn back in a few thousand years.

tritiya.short: The 3rd lunar day of each half-month: tithi 3 (bright half) and tithi 18 (dark half).
full: Tritiya means “third”. It is the 3rd tithi of both halves of the lunar month: in the bright half the Moon is 24° to 36° ahead of the Sun, in the dark half 204° to 216°.
Almanacs name Gauri as its ruling god.

tropical-longitude.short: A longitude measured from the spring equinox, as Western almanacs do. Equals the text's longitude plus the ayanamsha.
full: The text measures longitudes from a fixed point among the stars (sidereal). Western astronomy measures them from the spring equinox (tropical). The two differ by the ayanamsha.
The Tropical lon column adds the text's own ayanamsha to the sidereal longitude, so you can compare with a modern almanac.

true-longitude.short: A planet's actual place along the zodiac after all the text's corrections are applied to its mean place.
full: The true longitude, sphuta, is where the planet really appears. For the Sun and Moon one correction is needed, for the apsis (manda). For Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus and Saturn the text applies four steps, mixing half and whole corrections for the apsis and for the sighrocca.
The True longitude column in Planet Positions is this value, measured on the star-fixed (sidereal) zodiac.

tula.short: The 7th sign, Libra (the balance): 180° to 210° of the star-fixed zodiac.
full: Tula is the sign the West calls Libra, the balance. In the text it covers 180° to 210° of the sidereal zodiac, which is offset from the Western sign of the same name by the ayanamsha. Its ruling planet is Venus.
It holds nakshatras 14 to 16, split into nine padas.

ujjain.short: The city in central India on the text's prime meridian, and the app's default location.
full: The text measures longitude on Earth from a line running from Lanka (on the equator) north through Ujjain, then called Avanti, to Meru at the pole. Planet places computed by the text are for midnight at Ujjain.
Ujjain lies at about 23.18° N, 75.78° E. Places east or west of it need the desantara correction.

uttara-ashadha.short: The 21st nakshatra, 266°40′ to 280° of the zodiac. Its name means “the latter unconquered”.
full: Uttara Ashadha spans 266°40′ to 280° of the sidereal zodiac, in Sagittarius. Its name means “the latter unconquered”, and its ruling god is the Vishvedevas, all the gods. Its junction star is usually identified with σ Sagittarii.

uttara-bhadrapada.short: The 26th nakshatra, 333°20′ to 346°40′ of the zodiac. Its name means “the latter lucky feet”.
full: Uttara Bhadrapada spans 333°20′ to 346°40′ of the sidereal zodiac, in Pisces. Its name means “the latter lucky feet”, and its ruling god is Ahirbudhnya, the serpent of the deep. Its junction star is usually identified with γ Pegasi.

uttara-phalguni.short: The 12th nakshatra, 146°40′ to 160° of the zodiac. Its name means “the latter reddish one”.
full: Uttara Phalguni spans 146°40′ to 160° of the sidereal zodiac, in Leo. Its name means “the latter reddish one”, and its ruling god is Aryaman, god of friendship. Its junction star is usually identified with Denebola (β Leonis).

vadavamukha.short: The text's South Pole, opposite Meru, where the demons live.
full: Vadavamukha means “mare's mouth”, an undersea fire of legend. The text places it at the southern end of the Earth's axis, below the ocean.

vaidhrita.short: The pata when the Sun's and Moon's longitudes sum to about 360° and their declinations are equal but opposite.
full: As a pata, vaidhrita happens when the Sun's and Moon's longitudes add up to about 360°, one on each side of the equator with the same declination.
Vaidhriti, the 27th and last yoga, covers the same stretch of the Sun and Moon's summed longitude.

vaishakha.short: The 2nd lunar month, about April–May. Named after Vishakha, near which its full moon falls.
full: Vaishakha is the 2nd month of the lunar year, falling about April–May. Its name comes from the nakshatra Vishakha: the full moon of this month falls near it.
When a leap month is added, it takes the name of the month that follows it.

vajra.short: The 15th of the 27 yogas: the Sun's and Moon's longitudes sum to 186°40′–200°. Means “thunderbolt” or “diamond”.
full: Vajra is the 15th yoga, in force while the Sun's and Moon's longitudes add up to between 186°40′ and 200°. Its name means “thunderbolt” or “diamond”.

valana.short: A tilt angle. In eclipses, how the path of contact leans; for the Moon, how its horns tilt against the horizon.
full: Valana means “deflection”. In an eclipse drawing it turns the east–west line to show from which side the shadow touches the disc. In Chapter 10 it gives the lean of the crescent's horns, which way up the Moon looks.
The Moon page shows it as Horn tilt: 0° means the horns point straight up and down.

image.alt: A crescent Moon whose line from horn to horn leans away from the vertical by an angle labelled valana.

vanija.short: The 6th of the seven movable karanas, which repeat eight times each lunar month.
full: Vanija is one of the seven ‘movable’ karanas. After Kimstughna opens the month, the seven follow one another in a fixed order, Bava, Balava, Kaulava, Taitila, Garaja, Vanija, Vishti, eight times over. Each lasts half a tithi, the time the Moon takes to gain 6° on the Sun.

vara.short: The day of the week. The text finds it from the day count, since the Kali epoch began on a Friday.
full: The seven weekdays are named after the seven planets, each ruling one day. The text's order of rulers comes from the planets' distances: count every fourth planet down the list Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, Moon.
The week is one of the five parts of the panchanga.

equations.caption: A = ahargana from the Kali epoch; 0 = Sunday. The epoch was a Friday.

variyan.short: The 18th of the 27 yogas: the Sun's and Moon's longitudes sum to 226°40′–240°. Means “most excellent”.
full: Variyan is the 18th yoga, in force while the Sun's and Moon's longitudes add up to between 226°40′ and 240°. Its name means “most excellent”.

varsha-ritu.short: Varsha, the rains: the season while the Sun is in Cancer and Leo, about mid-July to mid-September.
full: Varsha means the rains. It lasts two solar months, while the Sun passes through Cancer and Leo, roughly mid-July to mid-September. The text begins the round of six seasons when the Sun enters Capricorn.

vasanta.short: Vasanta, spring: the season while the Sun is in Pisces and Aries, about mid-March to mid-May.
full: Vasanta means spring. It lasts two solar months, while the Sun passes through Pisces and Aries, roughly mid-March to mid-May. The text begins the round of six seasons when the Sun enters Capricorn.

venus.short: Venus, the brightest of the star-planets. It is only seen as a morning or evening star.
full: Its mean place is the mean Sun; its own circuit is given as its sighrocca's 7,022,376 turns in a Great Age.
Being so bright, it can be seen only 8° to 10° from the Sun, closer than any other planet.
It rules Friday.

vibhava.short: Year 2 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “plenty”.
full: Vibhava is year 2 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 36. Its name means “plenty”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

vijaya.short: Year 27 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “victory”.
full: Vijaya is year 27 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 1. Its name means “victory”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

vikari.short: Year 33 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “changing”.
full: Vikari is year 33 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 7. Its name means “changing”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

vikrama.short: Year 14 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “valour”.
full: Vikrama is year 14 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 48. Its name means “valour”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

vikruta.short: Year 24 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “changed”.
full: Vikruta is year 24 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 58. Its name means “changed”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

vilambi.short: Year 32 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “slow”.
full: Vilambi is year 32 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 6. Its name means “slow”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

vipala.short: A tiny unit of time used in almanacs: one sixtieth of a pala, or 0.4 seconds.
full: Almanacs split each pala into 60 vipalas when they want great precision. The text itself stops at the prana (4 seconds); the vipala is a later addition.

virodhi.short: Year 23 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “opponent”.
full: Virodhi is year 23 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 57. Its name means “opponent”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

virodhikrut.short: Year 45 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “causer of strife”.
full: Virodhikrut is year 45 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 19. Its name means “causer of strife”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

vishakha.short: The 16th nakshatra, 200° to 213°20′ of the zodiac. Its name means “forked”.
full: Vishakha spans 200° to 213°20′ of the sidereal zodiac, in Libra. Its name means “forked”, and its ruling god is Indra and Agni together. Its junction star is usually identified with ι Librae.

vishkambha.short: The 1st of the 27 yogas: the Sun's and Moon's longitudes sum to 0°–13°20′. Means “support”.
full: Vishkambha is the 1st yoga, in force while the Sun's and Moon's longitudes add up to between 0° and 13°20′. Its name means “support”.

vishti.short: The 7th of the seven movable karanas, which repeat eight times each lunar month.
full: Vishti is one of the seven ‘movable’ karanas. After Kimstughna opens the month, the seven follow one another in a fixed order, Bava, Balava, Kaulava, Taitila, Garaja, Vanija, Vishti, eight times over. Each lasts half a tithi, the time the Moon takes to gain 6° on the Sun.
Vishti, also called Bhadra, is avoided for new undertakings in almanac tradition.

vishvavasu.short: Year 39 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “wealth of all”.
full: Vishvavasu is year 39 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 13. Its name means “wealth of all”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

visibility-arc.short: How far from the Sun a body must be before it can be seen: 11° for Jupiter, 15° for Saturn, 17° for Mars.
full: The text calls these the kalamsha, the ‘degrees of time’. Jupiter needs 11°, Saturn 15°, Mars 17°, Mercury 12° or 14°, and Venus 8° or 10°. Bright stars need about 13°; the faintest nakshatra stars need up to 21°.
The text measures this distance as rising time, the time between the body and the Sun crossing the horizon. The app uses the simpler distance along the ecliptic as an approximation.

vriddhi.short: The 11th of the 27 yogas: the Sun's and Moon's longitudes sum to 133°20′–146°40′. Means “growth”.
full: Vriddhi is the 11th yoga, in force while the Sun's and Moon's longitudes add up to between 133°20′ and 146°40′. Its name means “growth”.

vrishabha.short: The 2nd sign, Taurus (the bull): 30° to 60° of the star-fixed zodiac.
full: Vrishabha is the sign the West calls Taurus, the bull. In the text it covers 30° to 60° of the sidereal zodiac, which is offset from the Western sign of the same name by the ayanamsha. Its ruling planet is Venus.
It holds nakshatras 3 to 5, split into nine padas.

vrishapriya.short: Year 15 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “fond of the bull”.
full: Vrishapriya is year 15 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 49. Its name means “fond of the bull”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

vrishchika.short: The 8th sign, Scorpio (the scorpion): 210° to 240° of the star-fixed zodiac.
full: Vrishchika is the sign the West calls Scorpio, the scorpion. In the text it covers 210° to 240° of the sidereal zodiac, which is offset from the Western sign of the same name by the ayanamsha. Its ruling planet is Mars.
It holds nakshatras 16 to 18, split into nine padas.

vyaghata.short: The 13th of the 27 yogas: the Sun's and Moon's longitudes sum to 160°–173°20′. Means “a blow”.
full: Vyaghata is the 13th yoga, in force while the Sun's and Moon's longitudes add up to between 160° and 173°20′. Its name means “a blow”.

vyatipata.short: The pata when the Sun and Moon are on the same side of the equator at equal declination, their longitudes summing to about 180°.
full: As a pata, vyatipata happens when the Sun's and Moon's longitudes add up to about 180° and their declinations are equal. The Nominal (sum rule) column gives that rough time; the app then finds the moment the declinations truly match.
Vyatipata is also the 17th of the 27 yogas, the one in force when the sum of the Sun's and Moon's longitudes is near 180°.

vyaya.short: Year 20 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “spending”.
full: Vyaya is year 20 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 54. Its name means “spending”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

waning.short: Shrinking. The Moon wanes from full moon to new moon, during the dark half of the month.
full: While the Moon's elongation goes from 180° back to 360°, the lit part shrinks. This is the dark half, krishna paksha. The Moon then rises later each night and is seen in the morning.

waxing.short: Growing. The Moon waxes from new moon to full moon, during the bright half of the month.
full: While the Moon's elongation goes from 0° to 180°, the lit part grows each night. This is the bright half, shukla paksha. The lit side faces west, toward the setting Sun.

wheel.short: A graduated ring hung upright facing the Sun. The shadow of its axle shows how high the Sun is.
full: The wheel, cakra, is marked in degrees round its edge. Hung so its face points to the Sun, the shadow of a pin at its centre falls on the Sun's altitude, and the time follows. The details come from Burgess's notes.

yamakoti.short: An imagined city on the equator, a quarter of the way round the Earth east of Lanka.
full: The text places four cities on the equator, 90° apart: Lanka on Ujjain's meridian, Yamakoti to the east, Siddhapura opposite and Romaka to the west. When the Sun is overhead at one, it is rising, setting or at midnight at the others.

yoga.short: One of 27 steps of 13°20′ in the sum of the Sun's and Moon's longitudes. One of the panchanga's five parts.
full: Add the Sun's and the Moon's longitudes and divide the total into steps of 13°20′, the width of a nakshatra. Each step is a yoga, with its own name, from Vishkambha to Vaidhriti. A yoga lasts roughly a day.
The word yoga also means “joining”. The text uses it for a planet meeting a star as well.

yojana.short: The text's unit of distance. The Earth is 1,600 yojanas across, which makes a yojana roughly 8 km.
full: The yojana was a traditional Indian measure of road distance. The text gives every size and orbit in yojanas: the Earth's diameter is 1,600, the Moon's 480, the Sun's 6,500, and the Moon's orbit 324,000.

Measured against the real Earth, a yojana comes to about 8 km (5 miles). The text's distances to the planets are not modern ones; they come from its own rule that every planet moves the same distance each day.

yuva.short: Year 9 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle (counting from Prabhava). The name means “youth”.
full: Yuva is year 9 of the 60-year Jupiter cycle, counting from Prabhava as most almanacs and this app do. The text itself counts from Vijaya, which makes it year 43. Its name means “youth”.
Each Jupiter year is the time Jupiter takes to move through one sign, about 361 days, so the cycle slowly slips against the solar calendar.

zodiac.short: The band of sky the Sun, Moon and planets move through, split into 12 signs and 27 nakshatras. Fixed to the stars here.
full: The zodiac is a circle of 360° around the sky, centred on the Sun's yearly path. The text divides it two ways: into 12 signs (rashis) of 30° each, and into 27 nakshatras of 13°20′ each.
The text's zodiac is sidereal: it starts at a fixed point among the stars, near the star Revati. So a planet's longitude here is its sidereal longitude.
